issues.legal_issue: Restitution is unavailable when a sale made under a reversed decree would also have occurred under the restored decree because the debtor defaulted on its payment terms.
material_facts: A decree was amended to reduce the debt and permit payment in annual instalments, with the whole balance becoming due upon default of three instalments.
The debtor did not obtain a stay of the amended decree while it was under challenge and paid none of the instalments that fell due.
The debtor did not pay or offer to pay an instalment to avoid default, or obtain an order excusing or altering the payment terms.
The decreeholder executed a sale after the third instalment had gone unpaid.
The Privy Council later restored the amended decree without changing its instalment terms or extending the time for payment.
The debtor did not establish that he could have paid the accumulated instalments or otherwise prevented the sale under the restored decree.
issues.conclusion: The debtor was not entitled to restitution of the property or mesne profits because the sale was inevitable under the restored decree and was not in substance a consequence of the decree later reversed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, restitution ordinarily requires a party who benefited from an erroneous judgment to restore what the other party lost, but the court must not order restitution where doing so would be contrary to the real justice of the case. A judgment-debtor is not entitled to recover property unless the sale was in substance and truth a consequence of the error in the reversed decree: Dayal Sardar v. Tari Deshi (I.L.R. 59 Cal. 647), approved. Where the debtor could not have paid the reduced decretal amount and the sale would not have been avoided by an earlier modification, restitution is unavailable: Gansu Ram v. Parvati Kuer (A.I.R. 1941 Pat. 130), approved.

rule.if: restitution_after_decree_reversal_proceeding and installment_payment_decree_restored and debtor_did_not_obtain_stay and required_installments_went_unpaid and sale_would_have_occurred_under_restored_decree

predicates.restitution_after_decree_reversal_procee: The matter is a proceeding seeking restitution after a decree has been reversed or altered.
predicates.installment_payment_decree_restored: The court restored a decree that permitted payment in instalments and made the remaining debt payable upon specified defaults.
predicates.debtor_did_not_obtain_stay: The debtor obtained no order suspending the operation of the decree while it was under challenge.
predicates.required_installments_went_unpaid: The debtor failed to pay the instalments whose non-payment triggered the decree's default terms.
predicates.sale_would_have_occurred_under_restored_: The sale would have proceeded under the restored decree even if that decree had been in force at the time of sale.

issues.definition: When a restitution proceeding follows a decree's reversal and the restored instalment decree would still have led to the sale after the debtor's unpaid instalments, restitution is not granted.

issues.legal_issue: A sale in execution is not invalidated by later estate-administration proceedings when earlier proceedings were quashed before the sale and a later application is treated as fresh.
material_facts: The debtor had applied for administration of his estate under the applicable legislation, but the Board of Revenue quashed those proceedings before the execution sale.
No application for administration was pending when the execution sale took place.
After the sale, legislation allowed applications whose proceedings had previously been quashed to be amended, and the debtor applied to amend his earlier application.
The courts treated the later application as a fresh application and the related proceedings as starting afresh.
issues.conclusion: The sale was unaffected by the statutory bar because no application was pending when it occurred, and the later fresh application had no retrospective effect on its validity.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 6 and 7 of the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act, 1934, as amended by the U.P. Encumbered Estates (Amendment) Act, 1939, proceedings that had been quashed before a sale did not impose a bar on that sale. An order on a later application treated as a fresh application under section 4 did not operate retrospectively to affect a sale made when no such application was pending. The court also noted that the debtor could not relitigate whether the proceedings should be treated as pending in light of the earlier decision in his case.

rule.if: execution_sale_dispute and earlier_estate_proceedings_quashed_before_sale and no_estate_application_pending_at_sale and later_application_treated_as_fresh

predicates.execution_sale_dispute: The matter concerns the validity of a sale made in execution of a decree.
predicates.earlier_estate_proceedings_quashed_befor: The estate-administration proceedings initiated before the sale were quashed before the sale occurred.
predicates.no_estate_application_pending_at_sale: No application for estate administration was pending when the execution sale occurred.
predicates.later_application_treated_as_fresh: An application made after the sale was treated by the court as a new application rather than as a continuation of the earlier proceedings.

issues.definition: In a dispute over an execution sale, if earlier estate proceedings were quashed before the sale, no application was pending at the sale, and a later application was treated as fresh, the sale is unaffected by the later proceedings.
